atlas.gpu.title: GPU
atlas.gpu.summary: A throughput processor: thousands of simple lanes that hide latency with parallelism instead of caches and prediction.
atlas.gpu.body:
A CPU spends its transistors making *one* thread fast: deep caches, branch prediction, out-of-order execution. A GPU spends them on **many** lanes of arithmetic. It hides memory latency by keeping thousands of threads in flight and switching between them for free.

For ML and HPC that trade is ideal. The work is mostly dense linear algebra, the same operation over huge arrays. A data-center GPU such as the H100 pairs ~130 [[streaming-multiprocessor|streaming multiprocessors]] with [[tensor-core|tensor cores]] and 80 GB of [[hbm|HBM]] at several TB/s.

**What makes a GPU fast in practice**
- Enough parallel work to fill every SM (see [[occupancy]]).
- Arithmetic intensity high enough to be compute-bound, not memory-bound (see [[roofline]]).
- Data that stays on the device. PCIe transfers are ~50× slower than HBM.

In a cluster, the GPU is one node in a hierarchy: GPU → [[nvlink]] within a server → [[infiniband]] between servers. Most cluster engineering is about keeping that hierarchy busy.
atlas.streaming-multiprocessor.title: Streaming Multiprocessor (SM)
atlas.streaming-multiprocessor.summary: The GPU's core building block: schedulers, registers, shared memory, CUDA cores and tensor cores.
atlas.streaming-multiprocessor.body:
An SM is roughly what a "core" is on a CPU, but built for throughput. Each SM has warp schedulers, a large register file, configurable **shared memory / L1** and execution units: FP32/INT "CUDA cores", special-function units and [[tensor-core|tensor cores]].

A kernel launch is split into **thread blocks**. Each block lands on one SM and stays there. The SM interleaves the [[warp|warps]] of all resident blocks every cycle, so when one warp waits on memory another issues.

**Why you care as an operator**
- SM count × clock sets peak FLOP/s. A GPU throttled to 55% clock (thermal or power) delivers ~55% of the math. See [[power-and-thermals]].
- `DCGM_FI_PROF_SM_ACTIVE` and `SM_OCCUPANCY` (from [[dcgm]]) tell you whether SMs are actually busy. "GPU utilization" in [[nvidia-smi]] only means *some* kernel was running, not that every SM was.
atlas.warp.title: Warp & SIMT
atlas.warp.summary: 32 threads that execute in lockstep. Divergent branches and scattered memory access cost real performance.
atlas.warp.body:
NVIDIA GPUs execute threads in groups of **32 called warps**. This is *Single Instruction, Multiple Threads* (SIMT): the warp shares one instruction stream, while each thread has its own registers.

Two consequences dominate kernel performance:

1. **Branch divergence**: if threads in a warp take different paths of an `if`, the warp runs *both* paths with lanes masked off. Keep control flow uniform within a warp where you can.
2. **Memory coalescing**: when the 32 threads read adjacent addresses, the hardware merges them into a few wide transactions. Scattered access multiplies memory traffic. See [[memory-coalescing]].

Warps are also the unit the scheduler juggles to hide latency. More resident warps (higher [[occupancy]]) gives it more choices, up to the point where registers and shared memory run out.
atlas.tensor-core.title: Tensor Core
atlas.tensor-core.summary: Matrix-multiply-accumulate units that deliver most of a modern GPU's FLOPs, if you feed them the right precision and shapes.
atlas.tensor-core.body:
Tensor cores compute small matrix products (e.g. 16×16 tiles) in one instruction. On an H100 they deliver ~989 dense BF16 TFLOP/s versus ~67 TFLOP/s of plain FP32. That gap is why [[mixed-precision]] training is the default.

**Getting the FLOPs**
- Use BF16/FP16 (or FP8 with Transformer Engine) for matmuls. FP32 without TF32 never touches them.
- Keep GEMM dimensions large and multiples of 8/16. Tiny micro-batches or very narrow [[tensor-parallelism|tensor-parallel]] shards make small GEMMs that can't saturate the units.
- Keep data flowing from [[hbm]]. Tensor cores are so fast that many ops (normalization, activations, attention softmax) become memory-bound. Kernel fusion such as FlashAttention exists for this.

Model FLOPs Utilization ([[mfu]]) is ultimately a measure of how busy the tensor cores are.
atlas.hbm.title: HBM & the memory hierarchy
atlas.hbm.summary: High Bandwidth Memory: stacked DRAM next to the GPU die. Its capacity bounds model size and its bandwidth bounds many kernels.
atlas.hbm.body:
High Bandwidth Memory stacks DRAM dies beside the GPU on a silicon interposer. An H100 SXM has 80 GB at ~3.35 TB/s. Below it sit L2 (tens of MB), per-SM shared memory/L1 and registers, each smaller and faster.

**Capacity** is the first wall in large-model training. Mixed-precision Adam needs ~16 bytes per parameter (weights, gradients, FP32 master copy and two moments), *before* activations. A 7B model needs ~107 GB of state alone, more than one GPU holds. That's why [[zero-fsdp|ZeRO/FSDP]], [[tensor-parallelism]] and [[activation-checkpointing]] exist.

**Bandwidth** is the second wall. Any kernel with low arithmetic intensity (elementwise ops, norms, small matmuls) is limited by HBM bandwidth, not FLOPs. See [[roofline]].

Try the calculator below: change the model, ZeRO stage and parallelism and watch the per-GPU footprint against the 80 GB line.
atlas.mig.title: Multi-Instance GPU (MIG)
atlas.mig.summary: Hardware partitioning of one GPU into up to seven isolated instances, each with its own SMs, L2 slices and memory.
atlas.mig.body:
MIG (A100, H100 and later) splits a GPU into up to **7 instances**. Each gets a dedicated slice of SMs, L2 cache and HBM, with its own memory controllers. Faults and memory pressure in one instance don't leak into another, which makes MIG the strongest of the GPU-sharing options. See [[multi-tenancy]].

Profiles are named by compute slices and memory, e.g. on an 80 GB H100: `1g.10gb`, `2g.20gb`, `3g.40gb`, `4g.40gb`, `7g.80gb`. Not every combination fits. Placement follows fixed rules about which slices can sit together.

**When to use it**: inference, notebooks and CI workloads that need a fraction of a GPU and *must not* interfere with each other. **When not to**: large training jobs. They want whole GPUs and NVLink, which MIG instances can't use for peer-to-peer.

Play with the partitioner below to see how profiles pack.
atlas.power-and-thermals.title: Power & thermals
atlas.power-and-thermals.summary: GPUs throttle clocks to stay under their power limit and temperature thresholds, and the slowest GPU sets the pace.
atlas.power-and-thermals.body:
Every GPU has a **power limit** (TDP; 700 W for H100 SXM) and **thermal thresholds**. When it would exceed either, firmware lowers clocks:

- **SW Power Cap**: drawing the configured limit; clocks drop slightly. Often intentional. See [[power-capping]].
- **HW Slowdown / HW Thermal Slowdown**: an emergency brake, typically from overheating (failed fan, blocked airflow, hot inlet air). Clocks can drop by half.

In synchronous training, one throttled GPU turns into a cluster-wide slowdown. Every collective waits for it. That's a [[stragglers|straggler]].

**Where to look**
- `nvidia-smi -q -d PERFORMANCE` shows "Clocks Event Reasons" (formerly *throttle reasons*).
- `nvidia-smi -q -d TEMPERATURE` shows current, slowdown and shutdown temperatures.
- [[dcgm]] fields such as `DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP`, `DCGM_FI_DEV_POWER_USAGE` and the clock-throttle bitmask feed alerting.
atlas.pcie.title: PCIe
atlas.pcie.summary: The general-purpose bus between CPU, GPU, NIC and NVMe. Ubiquitous, but an order of magnitude slower than NVLink.
atlas.pcie.body:
PCI Express connects GPUs to the host CPU, NICs and storage. A Gen5 x16 link moves ~64 GB/s per direction. Gen4 x16 moves ~32 GB/s. That's plenty for loading data, but slow for GPU-to-GPU traffic during training.

**Why it matters**
- GPUs without [[nvlink]] (e.g. L40S) must do all peer traffic over PCIe, often through the CPU's root complex. [[tensor-parallelism|Tensor parallelism]] suffers badly.
- **GPUDirect RDMA** lets a NIC read and write GPU memory directly over PCIe, skipping host memory. Good servers pair each GPU with a NIC under the same PCIe switch. Check with `nvidia-smi topo -m`.
- "Fallen off the bus" ([[xid-errors|Xid 79]]) is literally the GPU disappearing from PCIe.
atlas.nvlink.title: NVLink
atlas.nvlink.summary: NVIDIA's high-bandwidth GPU-to-GPU link: ~450 GB/s per direction per H100, roughly 7× PCIe Gen5.
atlas.nvlink.body:
NVLink is a point-to-point interconnect between GPUs. An H100 SXM has 18 NVLink 4 links totalling ~900 GB/s bidirectional (~450 GB/s each way). Through [[nvswitch]], all 8 GPUs in an HGX server talk to each other at full speed.

**Design rule**: put the *chattiest* parallelism on the fastest link. [[tensor-parallelism|Tensor parallelism]] does several all-reduces per layer, so it lives inside the NVLink domain. Data parallelism, which syncs once per step and overlaps with compute, can cross [[infiniband]].

**Failure mode**: NVLink errors appear as [[xid-errors|Xid 74]]. A degraded link forces traffic over PCIe and quietly slows collectives. `nvidia-smi nvlink -s` shows per-link status, and `all_reduce_perf` (nccl-tests) on an idle node shows the bandwidth drop.
atlas.nvswitch.title: NVSwitch
atlas.nvswitch.summary: A switch chip that gives every GPU in a server full-bandwidth NVLink to every other GPU.
atlas.nvswitch.body:
Without a switch, NVLink is point-to-point, so GPUs only connect to a few neighbors. **NVSwitch** builds a non-blocking crossbar: in an HGX H100 server, four NVSwitch chips connect all 8 GPUs all-to-all at full NVLink bandwidth.

Newer systems extend the NVLink domain *beyond* a server (e.g. NVL72 racks), so 72 GPUs act like one large tensor-parallel island. The rule from [[nvlink]] still applies: the bigger the NVLink domain, the larger the tensor-parallel or expert-parallel groups you can run without touching the slower scale-out network.

`nvidia-smi topo -m` shows `NV18` (18 bonded links) between every GPU pair in an NVSwitch system.
atlas.infiniband.title: InfiniBand & RoCE
atlas.infiniband.summary: The scale-out fabric: RDMA networks that move tensors between servers without involving the CPU.
atlas.infiniband.body:
Between servers, GPUs talk over a **scale-out network**. Two families dominate:

- **InfiniBand (IB)**: a purpose-built RDMA fabric. NDR runs 400 Gb/s per port with very low latency and credit-based lossless flow control.
- **RoCE v2**: RDMA over Converged Ethernet. Same verbs API over Ethernet. It needs careful configuration (PFC/ECN) to stay lossless, but it's cheaper and familiar to network teams.

Modern training servers attach **one 400G NIC per GPU** (rail-optimized), so each GPU gets ~50 GB/s of scale-out bandwidth via GPUDirect RDMA.

**Ops checklist**
- `ibstat` should show every port `Active` / `LinkUp` at the expected rate.
- [[nccl]] logs `NET/IB` when it uses RDMA and `NET/Socket` when it fell back to TCP, a classic silent 10× slowdown (often from `NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1` or a bad HCA config).
- A port going down mid-job hangs collectives until the NCCL watchdog times out.
atlas.cluster-topology.title: Cluster topology
atlas.cluster-topology.summary: How nodes, switches and links are wired: fat trees, rail-optimized designs, and why oversubscription bites collectives.
atlas.cluster-topology.body:
A GPU cluster network is usually a **fat tree**. Leaf switches connect servers, and spine switches connect leaves. If uplink capacity equals downlink capacity the fabric is **non-blocking** (1:1). Cheaper designs oversubscribe (e.g. 2:1), which is fine for web traffic and painful for all-reduce, where everyone transmits at once.

**Rail-optimized** designs wire NIC *i* of every server to the same leaf switch ("rail *i*"). NCCL's ring and tree algorithms then keep most traffic on one rail, one hop away.

**Rules of thumb**
- The bandwidth hierarchy (HBM ≫ NVLink ≫ IB ≫ storage) should map onto the parallelism hierarchy. See [[tensor-parallelism]], [[pipeline-parallelism]] and [[data-parallelism]].
- Keep spare capacity. A warm spare node turns a hardware failure into a requeue instead of an outage. See [[checkpointing]].
- Power and cooling are topology too. Racks have kW budgets, and liquid cooling changes what fits. See [[energy-and-carbon]].
atlas.cuda-stack.title: The CUDA software stack
atlas.cuda-stack.summary: Kernel driver → user-mode driver → CUDA runtime → libraries → frameworks. Version mismatches live at every seam.
atlas.cuda-stack.body:
From the bottom up:

1. **Kernel module** (`nvidia.ko` and friends). It owns the hardware, memory management (including Unified Memory / UVM), interrupts and error reporting. NVIDIA publishes an **open-source** version, *open-gpu-kernel-modules*, the default for Turing and newer GPUs. The [[xid-errors|Xid]] messages you read in `dmesg` come from here.
2. **User-mode driver** (`libcuda.so`): the CUDA *driver API*, shipped with the driver.
3. **CUDA runtime and toolkit** (`libcudart`, `nvcc`): what applications compile against.
4. **Libraries**: cuBLAS, cuDNN, [[nccl|NCCL]], CUTLASS.
5. **Frameworks**: PyTorch, JAX, plus higher-level tooling.

**Compatibility rule**: a newer driver runs older CUDA runtimes, but not the reverse. `nvidia-smi` prints the driver version and the *maximum* CUDA version it supports. Containers bundle their own runtime but must use the host's driver, injected by the NVIDIA Container Toolkit. See [[containers-and-gpus]].
atlas.cuda-streams.title: CUDA streams & async execution
atlas.cuda-streams.summary: Queues of GPU work that let copies, kernels and communication overlap instead of waiting on each other.
atlas.cuda-streams.body:
A **stream** is an ordered queue of GPU operations. Work in different streams can run concurrently: a host-to-device copy in one, a kernel in another, an NCCL collective in a third. **Events** express dependencies between streams without blocking the CPU.

This is the mechanism behind every "overlap" optimization:
- Gradient all-reduce overlapping with the backward pass in [[data-parallelism|DDP]] uses a separate communication stream.
- Prefetching the next batch while the current one computes (see [[input-pipeline]]).
- ZeRO-3/FSDP prefetching the next layer's parameters (see [[zero-fsdp]]).

Projects such as **grCUDA** go further. They build the dependency graph from the data each kernel touches and schedule independent kernels on separate streams automatically, so polyglot programs get concurrency without hand-written stream code.

*Pitfall*: any implicit synchronization (`cudaDeviceSynchronize`, `.item()` in PyTorch, pageable memory copies) collapses your carefully built overlap back into serial execution.
atlas.nccl.title: NCCL
atlas.nccl.summary: NVIDIA's collective communication library: topology-aware all-reduce, all-gather and friends over NVLink, PCIe and RDMA.
atlas.nccl.body:
NCCL ("nickel") implements the collectives distributed training runs on: all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, broadcast and send/recv. It discovers the topology (NVLink, NVSwitch, PCIe, NICs) and builds **rings** and **trees** to use it. See [[all-reduce]].

**Environment variables worth knowing**
- `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` prints the chosen transport and channels. Read it.
- `NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1` forces TCP sockets instead of InfiniBand. It's useful on laptops and a disaster in production.
- `NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME` / `NCCL_IB_HCA` select interfaces.

**Diagnosing**
- `all_reduce_perf` from *nccl-tests* measures achievable *bus bandwidth*. Run it on idle nodes to catch bad links before users do.
- Hung collectives end with a PyTorch **watchdog timeout**. The cause is usually one bad rank: a dead link, a lost GPU or a [[stragglers|straggler]] that stopped responding.
atlas.slurm.title: Slurm
atlas.slurm.summary: The batch scheduler that runs most HPC and many AI clusters: partitions, jobs, allocations and node states.
atlas.slurm.body:
Slurm turns a pile of servers into a shared machine. Key concepts:

- **Partitions**: named groups of nodes with limits (`sinfo` lists them).
- **Jobs** are submitted with `sbatch script.sh`. `#SBATCH` lines in the script request resources: `--nodes`, `--gpus-per-node`, `--time`, `--partition`.
- **Allocation**: the scheduler picks nodes (backfill, priority, [[fair-share]]) and runs the script on the first one. `srun` launches tasks across the rest.
- **Node states**: `idle`, `alloc`, `drain` (finish current work, take no new work) and `down`.

**Daily operator commands**
```
squeue --me                       # what's running / pending and why
sacct                             # history with exit codes
scontrol show job <id>            # everything about a job
scontrol update NodeName=node-3 State=DRAIN Reason="gpu5 fan"
sinfo -R                          # why nodes are drained
scontrol requeue <id>             # restart a job (from its checkpoint)
```
Draining with a clear reason is the polite way to say "this hardware is suspect" without killing anyone's job.
atlas.kubernetes-gpu.title: Kubernetes & the GPU Operator
atlas.kubernetes-gpu.summary: Running GPU workloads on Kubernetes: device plugins, the GPU Operator, MIG profiles and gang scheduling.
atlas.kubernetes-gpu.body:
Kubernetes doesn't know about GPUs by default. The **NVIDIA device plugin** advertises `nvidia.com/gpu` as a schedulable resource. The **GPU Operator** installs and manages the whole stack as containers: driver, container toolkit, device plugin, [[dcgm|DCGM exporter]] and MIG manager.

**Differences from [[slurm]] that matter for training**
- Kubernetes schedules *pods* one at a time. Distributed training needs **gang scheduling** (all-or-nothing), provided by add-ons such as Kueue or Volcano.
- Topology awareness (same rack, same NVLink domain) needs extra configuration.
- It excels at mixed fleets: inference services, notebooks and CI next to batch jobs, often on [[mig|MIG]] slices.

Many organizations run both: Slurm for large training, Kubernetes for everything else, sometimes on the same hardware.
atlas.containers-and-gpus.title: Containers & GPUs
atlas.containers-and-gpus.summary: How containers get GPU access: the host driver, injected device nodes and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit.
atlas.containers-and-gpus.body:
A container image carries the CUDA *runtime* and libraries, but the GPU *driver* must come from the host (it's a kernel module). The **NVIDIA Container Toolkit** bridges the two. At start it mounts the driver's user-space libraries and the `/dev/nvidia*` device nodes into the container.

**Practical rules**
- Pin images to a CUDA version the host driver supports (see [[cuda-stack]]).
- HPC sites often use **Enroot/Pyxis** or **Apptainer** with Slurm. They run images unprivileged, which is a big security win.
- Never run training containers `--privileged`. Device access should be granted narrowly by the runtime.

**Security angle**: the device nodes *are* the GPU. Anything that can open `/dev/nvidia*` outside the scheduler's control can use the GPU. That's exactly how an unauthorized miner hides in plain sight. See [[cryptojacking]] and [[multi-tenancy]].
atlas.data-parallelism.title: Data parallelism (DDP)
atlas.data-parallelism.summary: Every GPU holds a full model replica, processes different data and averages gradients each step.
atlas.data-parallelism.body:
The simplest way to scale: replicate the model on *N* GPUs, give each a different slice of the batch, then **all-reduce the gradients** so every replica takes the same optimizer step.

**Cost**: one all-reduce of the full gradient (2 bytes × params in BF16) per step. With [[all-reduce|ring all-reduce]] the per-GPU traffic is ~2× the gradient size, *independent of N*. That's why data parallelism scales so well.

**Making it fast**
- **Overlap**: DDP buckets gradients and all-reduces each bucket as soon as backward produces it, hiding communication behind compute (see [[cuda-streams]]).
- **Gradient accumulation**: run several micro-batches before syncing. You get a bigger global batch with the same memory and fewer syncs per token.

**Limit**: every GPU must hold the *whole* model state. Once that stops fitting, see [[zero-fsdp]], [[tensor-parallelism]] and [[pipeline-parallelism]].
atlas.all-reduce.title: All-reduce (ring & tree)
atlas.all-reduce.summary: Sum a buffer across all ranks and give everyone the result. The collective that data-parallel training lives on.
atlas.all-reduce.body:
**Ring all-reduce** arranges *n* ranks in a ring and runs two phases (reduce-scatter, then all-gather) of *n−1* steps each. Every rank sends and receives ~2(n−1)/n × the buffer size:

```
T_ring ≈ 2(n−1)/n · S/B  +  2(n−1) · α
```

where *S* is bytes, *B* is per-link bandwidth and *α* is per-step latency. The bandwidth term barely grows with *n*. The latency term does, which hurts small messages at large scale.

**Tree** algorithms (NCCL's double binary tree) cut the latency term to ~log₂(n) steps and win for small messages and very large rank counts.

**Bus bandwidth**, the number nccl-tests reports, normalizes away the 2(n−1)/n factor, so you can compare it straight to link speed. A healthy NVLink node shows hundreds of GB/s. A node with a degraded link shows PCIe-class numbers.

Use the widget to see how size, rank count and bandwidth trade off.
atlas.tensor-parallelism.title: Tensor parallelism
atlas.tensor-parallelism.summary: Split each layer's matrices across GPUs (Megatron-style). Huge models fit, but every layer needs collectives.
atlas.tensor-parallelism.body:
Tensor parallelism (TP) shards the weight matrices *inside* each layer. In the Megatron-LM scheme, the first MLP matmul is split by columns and the second by rows, so a layer needs only **one all-reduce in forward and one in backward**. With attention handled the same way, that's ~4 activation all-reduces per transformer layer per micro-batch.

**Trade-offs**
- ✅ Weights, gradients, optimizer state *and* activations shrink by the TP degree.
- ❌ Communication is frequent, latency-sensitive and on the critical path. It mostly can't be hidden.
- ❌ Shards get narrow: hidden/TP too small means small GEMMs and lower [[tensor-core]] efficiency.

**Rule**: keep TP inside the [[nvlink]] domain (TP ≤ 8 on HGX servers). TP=16 across [[infiniband]] is a classic way to waste a cluster.
atlas.pipeline-parallelism.title: Pipeline parallelism
atlas.pipeline-parallelism.summary: Split the layer stack into stages on different GPUs and stream micro-batches through. Light traffic, but a bubble.
atlas.pipeline-parallelism.body:
Pipeline parallelism (PP) assigns contiguous layers to stages. Stage 1 runs layers 1–20, stage 2 runs 21–40, and so on. Only the activations at stage boundaries cross the network, so PP is comfortable spanning nodes over [[infiniband]].

**The bubble**: at the start and end of each step some stages sit idle while the pipeline fills and drains. With *p* stages and *m* micro-batches per step (1F1B schedule):

```
bubble fraction ≈ (p − 1) / (m + p − 1)
```

More micro-batches (gradient accumulation) shrink the bubble. Interleaved schedules shrink it further, at the cost of more communication.

**Constraints**: the layer count must divide evenly (or nearly) into stages, and stages should be balanced. The first stage also holds the most in-flight activations.

The classic large-model recipe, **3D parallelism**, combines all three: TP inside the node, PP across a few nodes, [[data-parallelism|DP]] (often with [[zero-fsdp|ZeRO-1]]) across everything else.
atlas.zero-fsdp.title: ZeRO & FSDP
atlas.zero-fsdp.summary: Shard optimizer state, gradients and parameters across data-parallel ranks instead of replicating them.
atlas.zero-fsdp.body:
Plain [[data-parallelism]] wastes memory: every rank stores identical copies of everything. **ZeRO** (and PyTorch's **FSDP**) shards it:

| Stage | Sharded | Per-GPU state (mixed-precision Adam) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | nothing | 16 B/param |
| 1 | optimizer states | 4 + 12/N B/param |
| 2 | + gradients | 2 + 14/N B/param |
| 3 / FSDP | + parameters | 16/N B/param |

**The catch with stage 3**: parameters must be **all-gathered** before each layer's forward *and* backward, every micro-batch. For a 70B model that's ~140 GB moved twice per micro-batch. On NVLink that's fine. Over a 400 Gb/s NIC it can dominate the step.

**Practical guidance**
- ZeRO-1 is nearly free and almost always worth it.
- ZeRO-3/FSDP is excellent within a node or on fast fabrics, and for fitting a model that otherwise wouldn't fit.
- At large scale, mix it: TP inside the node, ZeRO-1 or *hybrid sharding* (shard within a node, replicate across nodes).
atlas.mixed-precision.title: Mixed precision (BF16, FP8)
atlas.mixed-precision.summary: Do the math in 16- or 8-bit formats on tensor cores and keep an FP32 master copy for stable updates.
atlas.mixed-precision.body:
Mixed-precision training runs forward and backward in a low-precision format and keeps **FP32 master weights** for the optimizer update:

- **BF16** keeps FP32's exponent range, so it rarely needs loss scaling. It's the default on A100/H100.
- **FP16** needs dynamic **loss scaling** to keep small gradients from underflowing.
- **FP8** (H100+) roughly doubles matmul throughput again. Libraries like Transformer Engine manage per-tensor scaling.

**Why it's a big deal**: [[tensor-core|Tensor cores]] deliver ~15× more FLOP/s in BF16 than plain FP32 on H100. Training in FP32 leaves almost all of the GPU idle.

**Memory**: weights and gradients in 2 bytes, plus 12 bytes of FP32 optimizer state (master, Adam m, v) gives the "16 bytes per parameter" rule used throughout the Atlas.
atlas.activation-checkpointing.title: Activation checkpointing
atlas.activation-checkpointing.summary: Throw away activations during forward and recompute them in backward: trade ~33% more compute for far less memory.
atlas.activation-checkpointing.body:
Backpropagation needs the activations from the forward pass. For a transformer layer with FlashAttention that's roughly **34 · s · b · h bytes** (sequence × micro-batch × hidden), and it adds up fast. A 7B model at micro-batch 4 needs over 70 GB of activations.

**Checkpointing** (also called *recomputation*) keeps only each layer's input, then re-runs the layer's forward during backward. Cost: an extra forward pass, ~33% more compute (8N instead of 6N FLOPs per token). Benefit: activation memory drops to about **2 · s · b · h bytes per layer**.

**Use it when** activations are what's stopping you from fitting the model or a larger micro-batch. **Turn it off when** memory is fine. It's pure overhead then. Selective checkpointing (only the attention internals) gets most of the savings for a fraction of the cost.

Note that [[mfu|MFU]] deliberately doesn't count recomputed FLOPs, so checkpointing lowers MFU even though the GPU is just as busy.
atlas.roofline.title: Roofline model
atlas.roofline.summary: Attainable FLOP/s = min(peak compute, arithmetic intensity × memory bandwidth). Tells you which wall you're hitting.
atlas.roofline.body:
Every kernel has an **arithmetic intensity** (AI): FLOPs performed per byte moved from memory. The roofline says:

```
attainable FLOP/s = min( peak FLOP/s ,  AI × memory bandwidth )
```

Plot it on log-log axes and you get a slanted "memory roof" meeting a flat "compute roof" at the **ridge point**. For an H100 in BF16 that's ~989 TFLOP/s ÷ 3.35 TB/s ≈ **295 FLOPs/byte**.

- Elementwise ops (add, GELU, layer norm) have AI around 1. They're hopelessly memory-bound, so **fuse** them.
- Large matmuls have AI in the thousands. They're compute-bound, and that's where [[tensor-core|tensor cores]] shine.
- Attention without fusion is memory-bound. FlashAttention restructures it to stay on-chip.

The PRACE GPGPU guide uses the same reasoning for HPC kernels: first decide which roof you're under, then optimize for *that* resource.
atlas.mfu.title: MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization)
atlas.mfu.summary: Useful model FLOPs per second divided by the hardware's peak. The honest headline number for training efficiency.
atlas.mfu.body:
For dense transformers, training costs about **6 × parameters × tokens** FLOPs (2 forward + 4 backward). MFU compares what you achieved to the theoretical peak:

```
MFU = (6 · N · tokens_per_second) / (num_GPUs · peak_FLOP/s)
```

It deliberately ignores recomputation from [[activation-checkpointing]] (that's *HFU*, hardware FLOPs utilization), so it only rewards useful work.

**What's good?** 35–55% is typical for well-tuned large-model training on H100-class clusters. Above 60% is excellent.

**What drags it down**: small micro-batches, exposed communication (no overlap), pipeline bubbles, data-loader stalls, [[stragglers]], throttled clocks and plain FP32. The *Feed the Beast* mission walks through these in order.
atlas.scaling-efficiency.title: Scaling efficiency
atlas.scaling-efficiency.summary: Why 2× the GPUs rarely gives 2× the speed: serial work, communication and synchronization (Amdahl's law and friends).
atlas.scaling-efficiency.body:
**Amdahl's law**: if a fraction *s* of the work is serial, the speedup on *n* workers is at most 1 / (s + (1−s)/n). Even 5% serial work caps you at 20× speedup.

Distributed training adds **communication that grows with scale**: collective latency terms, cross-rack hops, and the growing chance that *some* GPU is slow (see [[stragglers]]).

**Weak vs strong scaling**
- *Strong scaling*: same problem, more GPUs. Efficiency drops as per-GPU work shrinks.
- *Weak scaling*: grow the batch with the GPU count. Much friendlier, which is why large-batch training exists, within the limits of what still converges.

**Measuring it**: scaling efficiency = (throughput at n) / (n × throughput at 1). Report it alongside [[mfu|MFU]]. A job can scale perfectly and still be inefficient per GPU.
atlas.memory-coalescing.title: Memory coalescing
atlas.memory-coalescing.summary: When a warp's 32 threads read adjacent addresses, the hardware merges them into a few wide transactions.
atlas.memory-coalescing.body:
Global memory is accessed in aligned segments (32-byte sectors, grouped into 128-byte lines). If the 32 threads of a [[warp]] read 32 consecutive 4-byte floats, the hardware serves them with **one** 128-byte transaction. If they read with a large stride, it may need **32** separate transactions, a 32× bandwidth penalty.

**Classic fixes from GPU programming practice (e.g. the PRACE guide)**
- Structure-of-arrays instead of array-of-structures.
- Have thread *i* touch element *i*, not *i × stride*.
- Stage awkward access patterns (transposes, stencils) through **shared memory**, then write out coalesced.
- Watch for shared-memory **bank conflicts** when you do.

Profilers (Nsight Compute) report "sectors per request". Ideal is 4 for 4-byte loads.
atlas.occupancy.title: Occupancy
atlas.occupancy.summary: Resident warps per SM as a fraction of the maximum: the scheduler's pool for hiding latency.
atlas.occupancy.body:
Each SM can host a limited number of warps (64 on H100). **Occupancy** is how many are actually resident, limited by each block's use of:

- **Registers** per thread (the register file is shared by all resident warps),
- **Shared memory** per block,
- **Threads** per block and blocks per SM.

Higher occupancy gives the warp scheduler more candidates to switch to while others wait on memory. But it's a means, not a goal. Many fast kernels (big GEMMs, FlashAttention) run at *low* occupancy, using registers and shared memory for data reuse instead.

**Practical approach** (from CUDA and PRACE best practice): use the occupancy calculator or Nsight Compute to see the limiting resource, try a few block sizes (multiples of 32), and measure. Don't assume.
atlas.input-pipeline.title: Input pipeline
atlas.input-pipeline.summary: Reading, decoding and tokenizing data fast enough to keep the GPUs fed: the bottleneck after you fix everything else.
atlas.input-pipeline.body:
Once the model math is fast, the CPU side often becomes the limit: reading shards from storage, decompressing, tokenizing, shuffling and collating batches.

**Symptoms**: GPU utilization saw-tooths, step time doesn't improve when you optimize the model, and logs show time waiting on the next batch.

**Fixes**
- More data-loader workers (processes) per rank, and pinned memory.
- **Prefetching**: prepare batch *k+1* while batch *k* trains (see [[cuda-streams]]).
- Pre-tokenize offline and store packed binary shards. It's the single biggest win for LLM pretraining.
- Make sure the parallel filesystem or object store can deliver the aggregate bandwidth: *GPUs × tokens/s × bytes per token*, plus checkpoint traffic.

The *Feed the Beast* mission shows the bottleneck moving to data loading the moment communication is fixed.
atlas.nvidia-smi.title: nvidia-smi
atlas.nvidia-smi.summary: The first tool you reach for: per-GPU utilization, memory, temperature, power, clocks, processes and configuration.
atlas.nvidia-smi.body:
`nvidia-smi` talks to the driver through NVML. The default table shows each GPU's temperature, power draw versus cap, memory use, utilization and the processes using it.

**The views that answer real questions**
```
nvidia-smi                                   # overview + processes
nvidia-smi -q -d PERFORMANCE                 # why are clocks low? (event reasons)
nvidia-smi -q -d TEMPERATURE,POWER,ECC       # thermals, power limits, memory errors
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,temperature.gpu,clocks.sm,power.draw --format=csv
nvidia-smi topo -m                           # NVLink/PCIe/NIC topology matrix
nvidia-smi nvlink -s                         # per-link NVLink status
sudo nvidia-smi -pl 500                      # set a power limit
```

**Caveat**: "GPU-Util" means *a kernel was running* during the sample window. It does not mean the GPU was busy. A GPU waiting at a barrier for a [[stragglers|straggler]] still spins. For real saturation metrics use [[dcgm]] profiling fields such as SM activity and tensor pipe activity.
atlas.dcgm.title: DCGM
atlas.dcgm.summary: Data Center GPU Manager: fleet-scale GPU telemetry, health checks, diagnostics and policy, the backbone of GPU monitoring.
atlas.dcgm.body:
DCGM runs a host engine (`nv-hostengine`) on each node and exposes:

- **Telemetry fields**: temperature, power, clocks, ECC, NVLink counters, Xid events and *profiling* metrics (`SM_ACTIVE`, `SM_OCCUPANCY`, `PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE`, `DRAM_ACTIVE`).
- **Health watches** that flag thermal, power, memory, PCIe and NVLink issues.
- **Diagnostics**: `dcgmi diag -r 1|2|3`, from quick deployment checks to stress tests. Run level 1 before a node rejoins the pool and level 3 after hardware work.
- **dcgm-exporter** for Prometheus, so it feeds Grafana dashboards and alert rules.

**Alerts worth having on day one**
- Any [[xid-errors|Xid]] event (critical ones page someone).
- HW thermal slowdown active for more than a minute.
- Uncorrectable [[ecc-errors|ECC]] or pending row remap.
- GPU busy while the scheduler shows *no job* on that node. That catches leaks *and* [[cryptojacking]].
atlas.xid-errors.title: Xid errors
atlas.xid-errors.summary: Error codes the NVIDIA kernel driver writes to the system log when something goes wrong on a GPU.
atlas.xid-errors.body:
An Xid is the driver's way of saying "this GPU had a problem". It appears in the kernel log (`dmesg`, `journalctl -k`) as `NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:xx:00.0): <code>, ...`. The messages are emitted by the kernel driver, which you can read in NVIDIA's *open-gpu-kernel-modules*.

**Codes every GPU operator should recognize**
| Xid | Meaning | Typical action |
|---|---|---|
| 13, 31, 43 | Application errors (bad memory access, illegal instruction) | Usually the user's code |
| 48 | Uncorrectable (double-bit) ECC error | Reset GPU, check row remapping, watch for repeats |
| 63, 64 | Row-remapping events | Reset when idle; RMA if remapping fails |
| 74 | NVLink error | Check links, reseat, run nccl-tests |
| 79 | GPU has fallen off the bus | Drain node, reboot, likely hardware ticket |
| 94, 95 | Contained / uncontained ECC error | Contained: affected app only. Uncontained: reset |

**Ops pattern**: alert on Xid via [[dcgm]], **drain** the node in [[slurm]] with the Xid in the reason, requeue affected jobs from their [[checkpointing|checkpoints]], then diagnose offline.
atlas.ecc-errors.title: ECC errors & row remapping
atlas.ecc-errors.summary: HBM is protected by error-correcting codes: single-bit errors are fixed silently, double-bit errors stop the work.
atlas.ecc-errors.body:
Data-center GPUs protect HBM (and on-chip SRAM) with ECC:

- **Single-bit (correctable)**: fixed on the fly and counted. A slowly growing count is normal. A rapidly growing one is a warning.
- **Double-bit (uncorrectable, DBE)**: the data is lost. The application gets an error ([[xid-errors|Xid 48]] / 94 / 95) and the GPU usually needs a **reset**.

A100 and later GPUs use **row remapping**: a bad DRAM row is replaced with a spare at the next GPU reset. `nvidia-smi -q -d ECC` shows "Remapped Rows → Pending: Yes" until you reset. If remapping *fails* (spares exhausted), the GPU needs replacing.

**Procedure**: drain → wait for jobs to leave → `nvidia-smi -r -i <gpu>` → `dcgmi diag -r 2` → return to service if clean.
atlas.stragglers.title: Stragglers
atlas.stragglers.summary: In synchronous training the whole job runs at the speed of its slowest GPU. Finding that GPU is a core ops skill.
atlas.stragglers.body:
Every collective is a barrier. If one of 1,024 GPUs runs 40% slower (a thermal throttle, a flaky link, a noisy neighbor or a slow disk on one node), **all 1,024** run 40% slower.

**Signatures**
- Throughput drops with no errors in the logs.
- Per-GPU utilization looks *inverted*: the straggler shows ~100%, the others less, because they idle at the barrier.
- The straggler's SM clock is low. `nvidia-smi -q -d PERFORMANCE` shows *HW Thermal Slowdown* or *SW Power Cap*.
- NCCL or framework timing shows one rank consistently arriving late to collectives.

**Response**: identify, drain, restart from a [[checkpointing|checkpoint]] on healthy hardware, and file a hardware ticket. At scale, automate it: continuous per-rank timing plus [[dcgm]] clocks and temperatures, and automatic cordoning.
atlas.checkpointing.title: Checkpointing & fault tolerance
atlas.checkpointing.summary: Periodically save model and optimizer state so a failure costs minutes of progress, not days.
atlas.checkpointing.body:
At thousands of GPUs, *something* fails every few hours. **Checkpointing** bounds the damage: on failure, you restart from the last saved state and lose at most one checkpoint interval.

**Choosing the interval**: too frequent wastes I/O time, too rare wastes compute on failure. A classic approximation (Young/Daly) is *interval ≈ √(2 × checkpoint_cost × MTBF)*.

**Making it cheap**
- Shard checkpoints: each rank writes its own slice in parallel.
- Async checkpointing: copy to host memory, then write in the background.
- Keep a few recent checkpoints. Corrupt or partial saves happen.

**Ops integration**: `scontrol requeue` or a job-level retry loop, plus a **warm spare** pool, turns "a GPU died" into a 5-minute blip. That's the loop you practice in *Fallen Off the Bus* and *The Slow Lane*.
atlas.multi-tenancy.title: Multi-tenancy & GPU sharing
atlas.multi-tenancy.summary: Time-slicing, MPS and MIG: three ways to share a GPU, with very different isolation guarantees.
atlas.multi-tenancy.body:
Shared clusters must decide how tenants share GPUs:

| Approach | Isolation | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| Whole-GPU allocation (scheduler-enforced) | Strong | Training, anything serious |
| [[mig\|MIG]] instances | Strong (hardware partitioned memory and SMs) | Inference, notebooks, CI |
| MPS (Multi-Process Service) | Weak: shared address-space faults can affect others | Cooperative jobs from one team |
| Time-slicing | None for memory; context switches | Dev and test only |

**Enforcement matters more than policy.** The scheduler should be the *only* path to a GPU: cgroup device controls restrict `/dev/nvidia*` to processes inside a job allocation. Without that, any user with a shell on a node can quietly use idle GPUs. See [[cryptojacking]].

Pair it with least-privilege accounts, no shared service users, audit logs and per-tenant accounting so usage is visible and fair (see [[fair-share]]).
atlas.cryptojacking.title: Cryptojacking on GPU clusters
atlas.cryptojacking.summary: Unauthorized cryptocurrency mining on stolen GPU time: the most common way GPU clusters get abused.
atlas.cryptojacking.body:
GPUs are valuable, and attackers who get code execution on a GPU node very often just **mine cryptocurrency**. Common entry points:

- Exposed, unauthenticated services: notebooks, dashboards and ML tooling UIs on `0.0.0.0` (see [[exposed-notebooks]]).
- Leaked credentials and API keys in images, repos or job scripts (see [[supply-chain-and-secrets]]).
- Over-privileged containers.

**Detection signals**
- A GPU busy with **no scheduled job**: compare [[dcgm]] utilization to scheduler state.
- Unknown process names on GPUs (`nvidia-smi`), often disguised as kernel threads.
- Outbound connections to mining pools (stratum protocol, ports like 3333/4444) in `ss -tnp` or firewall logs.
- New cron entries or systemd units owned by unexpected users.

**Response**: preserve evidence → kill the process → remove persistence → close the entry point → lock or rotate the affected identities → look for lateral movement → report. Killing the process alone is never enough. The *Night Shift* mission makes that concrete.
atlas.exposed-notebooks.title: Exposed notebooks & dashboards
atlas.exposed-notebooks.summary: A Jupyter server with no token on 0.0.0.0 is remote code execution for anyone who can reach it.
atlas.exposed-notebooks.body:
Jupyter is designed to run arbitrary code: that's the point. With `--ip=0.0.0.0` and authentication disabled (empty token and password), anyone who can reach the port can run commands as the notebook's user. The same applies to many ML dashboards, experiment trackers and inference UIs.

**Safer patterns**
- Bind to `127.0.0.1` and reach it through an **SSH tunnel** or an authenticated gateway (JupyterHub with SSO).
- Never disable tokens or passwords. Use TLS when traffic leaves the host.
- Firewall compute nodes: only the scheduler, monitoring and admin networks should reach them.
- Run notebooks *inside* scheduler allocations so they're time-limited and accounted.

**Detecting**: `ss -tlnp` shows listeners on `0.0.0.0`. Server logs record requests from unexpected IPs. Network monitoring flags inbound connections to compute nodes from outside.
atlas.supply-chain-and-secrets.title: Supply chain & secrets
atlas.supply-chain-and-secrets.summary: Container images, model weights and job scripts are code you run, and a common place for leaked credentials.
atlas.supply-chain-and-secrets.body:
A training job pulls in a lot of other people's code: base images, Python packages, custom kernels, pretrained weights and datasets. Each is part of your supply chain.

**Risks**
- Images with **baked-in secrets** (cloud keys, tokens) are readable by anyone who can pull them.
- **Pickle-based model files** can execute code when loaded. Prefer `safetensors`.
- Unpinned dependencies change underneath you.

**Controls**
- Pin images by digest, scan them, and build from trusted bases.
- Inject secrets at runtime from a secret manager, scoped per job. Never put them in `#SBATCH` scripts, env files in repos or image layers.
- Short-lived credentials and least privilege for storage access.
- Verify checksums or signatures for weights and datasets.

These controls protect *your* cluster and also the people whose data and models you're responsible for.
atlas.energy-and-carbon.title: Energy & carbon
atlas.energy-and-carbon.summary: kWh, PUE and CO₂e: measuring the environmental cost of compute so it can be managed, not guessed.
atlas.energy-and-carbon.body:
A GPU cluster is a power plant's customer. A rough accounting:

```
facility energy (kWh) = IT energy (GPUs + hosts + network) × PUE
emissions (kg CO₂e)   = facility energy × grid carbon intensity
```

- **PUE** (Power Usage Effectiveness) captures cooling and power-delivery overhead: ~1.1 for the best liquid-cooled sites, 1.3–1.6 for typical ones.
- **Carbon intensity** varies by more than 10× between regions and by time of day. Where and when you train can matter as much as how.

**Levers you control**
- Efficiency first: higher [[mfu|MFU]] means fewer GPU-hours for the same model.
- [[power-capping|Power caps]] trade a little speed for a lot of energy.
- Right-size: don't leave idle allocations running. Schedulers can reclaim them.
- Report kWh and CO₂e per run, next to cost and accuracy, so trade-offs are visible.

Every LazyLab run shows its energy, cost and carbon in the header.
atlas.power-capping.title: Power capping
atlas.power-capping.summary: Lower a GPU's power limit and give up a little speed for a lot less energy: often 20% less power for under 10% slower.
atlas.power-capping.body:
Near the top of the voltage/frequency curve, power grows much faster than performance: dynamic power ∝ *f·V²*, and voltage must rise with frequency. Capping power therefore costs proportionally *less* performance than it saves.

In training, only the compute-bound part of each step slows down. Communication, data loading and pipeline bubbles don't care about SM clocks, so the real-world throughput hit is smaller still.

**How**
```
sudo nvidia-smi -pl 550            # all GPUs on this node
sudo nvidia-smi -pl 550 -i 3       # just GPU 3
```
Caps reset on reboot unless managed by your provisioning or by [[dcgm]] policies.

**Caveats**: cap *all* GPUs in a job. Capping one creates a [[stragglers|straggler]]. And measure tokens per joule, not just tokens per second.
atlas.fair-share.title: Fair-share scheduling
atlas.fair-share.summary: Scheduler policies that balance access between teams based on what they're entitled to and what they've recently used.
atlas.fair-share.body:
On a shared cluster, "first come, first served" lets one team's 1,000 queued jobs starve everyone else. **Fair-share** scheduling (e.g. Slurm's multifactor priority) lowers the priority of users and accounts that recently used more than their share, with usage decaying over time.

**The ingredients**
- **Shares**: each account's entitlement, often matching funding or team size.
- **Usage decay**: a half-life (e.g. 7 days) so past usage is forgiven gradually.
- **QOS limits**: caps on concurrent GPUs, wall time or job count, so no single job blocks the cluster.
- **Preemption**: low-priority or opportunistic jobs can be checkpointed and requeued when priority work arrives. This only works if jobs [[checkpointing|checkpoint]] well.

Fairness is also about *transparency*: publish usage per team, queue wait times and energy, so allocation debates use data instead of anecdotes.
chapter.architecture.title: Anatomy of a GPU Cluster
chapter.architecture.kicker: From one streaming multiprocessor to a thousand-GPU fabric
chapter.architecture.intro: Before you can run, tune or secure a cluster you need a mental model of what's inside it. This chapter walks up the hierarchy: the GPU and its SMs, the memory that feeds them, the links between GPUs in a server, and the fabric between servers. Keep one idea in mind throughout: every level is roughly an order of magnitude slower than the one below it, and almost every design decision maps onto that ladder.
chapter.running.title: Running Jobs
chapter.running.kicker: Drivers, schedulers and the plumbing that gets work onto GPUs
chapter.running.intro: A cluster is only useful if people can get work onto it reliably and fairly. This chapter covers the software stack from kernel driver to framework, the batch scheduler most HPC and AI clusters run on, the communication library that makes multi-GPU training possible, and the habits (checkpoints, fair share) that keep a shared machine healthy.
chapter.monitoring.title: Watching the Fleet
chapter.monitoring.kicker: Telemetry, error codes and finding the one broken thing
chapter.monitoring.intro: At scale, something is always failing. This chapter is about seeing it: what nvidia-smi and DCGM can tell you, how the driver reports faults through Xid codes, what memory errors mean, and how a single throttled GPU can quietly slow a thousand others.
chapter.optimization.title: Making Training Fast
chapter.optimization.kicker: Kernels, precision and the parallelism zoo
chapter.optimization.intro: This is the longest chapter because it's where the money is. We start inside a single GPU (warps, memory access, tensor cores, precision), then scale out: data parallelism, overlap, memory tricks like checkpointing and ZeRO, and finally tensor and pipeline parallelism, the building blocks of 3D parallelism.
chapter.performance.title: Measuring and Scaling
chapter.performance.kicker: Rooflines, MFU, collectives and the price of a joule
chapter.performance.intro: How fast should this be? This chapter gives you the yardsticks: the roofline for kernels, MFU for training runs, the α-β model for collectives and Amdahl for scaling. It ends with the cost that is easiest to ignore, energy, and the simplest lever for it, power capping.
chapter.security.title: Securing Shared GPUs
chapter.security.kicker: Isolation, exposed services and incident response
chapter.security.intro: GPU clusters are shared, valuable and full of code nobody fully audited, which makes them attractive targets. This chapter covers how GPUs are shared and isolated, how containers get device access, and how the most common abuse (unauthorized mining through an exposed notebook) happens and is contained. Everything here is defensive.

mission.first-multinode.title: Two Nodes, One Job
mission.first-multinode.tagline: Your first multi-node training job won't even submit. Fix the batch script.
mission.first-multinode.briefing:
A researcher left you **train.sh**: a 7B training run that should use **2 nodes × 8 H100s**. They say "it just errors out." Get it running across both nodes, and make sure the nodes talk over **InfiniBand**, not the slow management Ethernet.

Useful commands: `cat train.sh`, `nano train.sh`, `sinfo`, `sbatch train.sh`, `squeue`, `cat slurm-<jobid>.out`.
mission.first-multinode.debrief:
**What you fixed**

1. **Partition**: Slurm rejects unknown partitions at submit time. `sinfo` is the source of truth.
2. **GPUs per node**: `--gpus-per-node` is *per node*. To get 16 GPUs, ask for 2 nodes × 8. Slurm refuses requests no node can ever satisfy ("Requested node configuration is not available").
3. **Transport**: with `NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1`, NCCL falls back to TCP sockets (~3 GB/s here) instead of RDMA over InfiniBand (~48 GB/s per GPU). The job "works" but runs at a quarter of its speed. The tell is in the NCCL INFO lines of the job log.

**Ops habit**: when a job runs but is slow, read the NCCL transport lines before tuning anything else.
mission.first-multinode.objective.0: A training job is running on 2 nodes × 8 GPUs
mission.first-multinode.hint.0: Run `sbatch train.sh` and read the error carefully. Then run `sinfo` to see which partitions really exist.
mission.first-multinode.hint.1: Each node has 8 GPUs, so `--gpus-per-node=16` can never be satisfied. Edit with `nano train.sh`, then Ctrl+S to save.
mission.first-multinode.hint.2: Once it runs, `cat slurm-<id>.out` shows `NET/Socket`: NCCL is using TCP because `NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1`. Delete that line, `scancel` the job and resubmit.
mission.fallen-off-bus.title: Fallen Off the Bus
mission.fallen-off-bus.tagline: A training job died overnight. Find the bad GPU, quarantine the node and get the run going again.
mission.fallen-off-bus.briefing:
Job **101** (a 7B run on 2 nodes) failed a few minutes ago and its owner is asking why. Your job:

- figure out **which node and GPU** killed it,
- **drain** that node so the scheduler stops placing work there,
- get the training job **running again** on healthy nodes.

Start with `sacct`, the job log (`cat slurm-101.out`) and the node's kernel log (`ssh <node>` then `dmesg`).
mission.fallen-off-bus.debrief:
**Xid 79: "GPU has fallen off the bus"** means the driver can no longer reach the GPU over PCIe. Causes include power, thermal or physical connection problems. Software can't fix it: the node needs a reboot at minimum, and often an RMA.

**The procedure you just ran**
1. *Triage from the scheduler*: `sacct` / the job log tells you *which* node.
2. *Confirm at the source*: `dmesg` holds the driver's Xid messages. The open-source NVIDIA kernel modules (open-gpu-kernel-modules) are where these are emitted.
3. *Contain*: **drain** the node (running jobs finish, new ones avoid it) with a reason the hardware team can read later in `sinfo -R`.
4. *Recover*: resubmit or requeue. The job resumes from its last checkpoint, so frequent checkpoints shrink the blast radius.

mission.straggler.title: The Slow Lane
mission.straggler.tagline: Throughput just halved across 32 GPUs, but nothing failed. Find the straggler.
mission.straggler.briefing:
A 7B run is training on **4 nodes (32 H100s)**, and **node-5** is idle as a spare. A few minutes ago tokens/s dropped by ~45%. No errors in the job log. Nothing crashed.

In synchronous data-parallel training, every step waits for the **slowest GPU**. Find it, take its node out of rotation and get MFU back above **60%**.

Tools: the dashboards on the right, `nvidia-smi`, `nvidia-smi -q -d PERFORMANCE`, `--query-gpu=index,temperature.gpu,clocks.sm`, `scontrol`.
mission.straggler.debrief:
**Stragglers are the silent killer of synchronous training.** One GPU throttled to ~55% clock made *all 32* GPUs wait at every all-reduce. That is a 45% throughput loss from a single fan.

**How to spot one**
- Per-GPU utilization looks *inverted*: the straggler is pegged at ~100%, while healthy GPUs show lower utilization because they idle at the barrier.
- Its SM clock is low and `Clocks Event Reasons` show **HW Thermal Slowdown**.
- DCGM metrics like `DCGM_FI_DEV_CLOCK_THROTTLE_REASONS` and temperature are what production alerting should key on.

**Fix**: take the hardware out of rotation (drain), restart from a checkpoint on healthy nodes, and file a ticket for the fan. A warm spare node is what made this recovery fast.
mission.straggler.objective.0: The node with the throttling GPU is drained
mission.straggler.objective.1: The training job is back above 60% MFU on healthy nodes
mission.straggler.hint.0: Look at the topology view: one GPU is hotter than the rest. Or check each node with `pdsh -w node-[1-4] nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,temperature.gpu,clocks.sm --format=csv`.
mission.straggler.hint.1: On node-3, `nvidia-smi -q -d PERFORMANCE -i 5` shows `HW Thermal Slowdown: Active`, and `-d TEMPERATURE` shows a failed chassis fan.
mission.straggler.hint.2: Drain node-3 with a reason, then `scontrol requeue 101`. The job restarts from its checkpoint on node-1,2,4,5.
mission.mfu-tune.title: Feed the Beast
mission.mfu-tune.tagline: 16 H100s running at 26% MFU. Tune the training config past 55% without running out of memory.
mission.mfu-tune.briefing:
Job **101** trains a 7B model on **2 nodes × 8 H100s**, but Model FLOPs Utilization is about **26%**. The config in **train.sh** was copied from a tiny debugging run.

Get the job to **≥ 55% MFU**. Every flag in the `train.py` line is fair game: `--micro-batch`, `--grad-accum`, `--overlap/--no-overlap`, `--ckpt/--no-ckpt`, `--workers`, `--precision`, `--zero`, `--tp`.

Workflow: `nano train.sh` → save → `scontrol requeue 101` (re-reads the script) → watch `tail slurm-101.out`. Look for OOM errors and the "dataloader wait" marker.
mission.mfu-tune.debrief:
**The bottleneck always moves.** You probably saw it shift from *communication* → *data loading* → *compute*:

- **Overlap**: DDP/FSDP can all-reduce gradient buckets while backward is still running. Without it, every byte of gradient sync is exposed time.
- **Activation checkpointing** trades ~33% extra compute for memory. It's essential for big models and pure waste when activations already fit.
- **Micro-batch size** sets GEMM sizes. Small GEMMs can't saturate tensor cores. Gradient accumulation lets you grow the *global* batch without growing memory.
- **Input pipeline**: once GPUs are fast, CPU-side tokenization becomes the limit. More workers, pre-tokenized data or prefetching fix it.

MFU (from the PaLM paper) counts only *useful* model FLOPs (6 × params × tokens), so recomputation never inflates it.
mission.mfu-tune.objective.0: The 7B job is training at ≥ 55% MFU
mission.mfu-tune.hint.0: Three things are slowing this job: tiny micro-batches, gradient sync that doesn't overlap with compute, and recomputation it doesn't need. Try `--overlap` and `--no-ckpt` first.
mission.mfu-tune.hint.1: After those fixes the bottleneck moves: the log shows `dataloader wait`. One worker can't feed 16 GPUs. Try `--workers 8`.
mission.mfu-tune.hint.2: A bigger `--micro-batch` (2) and `--grad-accum 4` keep tensor cores busy. Micro-batch 4 without checkpointing runs out of memory. Check the per-GPU memory line.
mission.power-cap.title: Watts Up
mission.power-cap.tagline: The facility asks for a 20% power cut. Keep at least 85% of the throughput.
mission.power-cap.briefing:
Facilities is running hot and asks every tenant to cut GPU power. Your well-tuned 7B job on **2 nodes × 8 H100s** draws ~675 W per GPU.

Bring the **average GPU power to ≤ 550 W** while keeping **≥ 85% of current tokens/s**.

GPU power limits are set per GPU with `sudo nvidia-smi -pl <watts>` on each node. `pdsh` can run a command on several nodes at once. Watch the power and throughput charts as you go.
mission.power-cap.debrief:
**Power capping is the cheapest efficiency win in the datacenter.**

GPU dynamic power scales roughly with *f·V²*, and voltage tracks frequency near the top of the curve. So the last ~10% of clock speed costs ~25% of the power. Also, only the *compute* part of a step slows down under a cap. Communication and data loading don't care about SM clocks.

Your result: roughly 20% less power for under 10% less throughput. That is **more tokens per joule**, which means lower cost and lower CO₂e per trained model. Many sites run training at 70–85% of TDP for exactly this reason.

**Responsible-ops lens**: energy is a shared resource. Reporting kWh and CO₂e per job (see the run's footer) helps teams make these trade-offs consciously.
mission.power-cap.hint.0: Power limits are per node: `ssh node-1`, `sudo nvidia-smi -pl 550`, `exit`, then the same on node-2. Or `sudo pdsh -w node-[1-2] nvidia-smi -pl 550`.
mission.power-cap.hint.1: Capping only one node slows the *whole* job, because the slowest GPU sets the pace, and barely moves the average. Cap both.
mission.power-cap.hint.2: Somewhere around 500–550 W keeps more than 85% of throughput. Go too low (≤ 450 W) and you fall under.
mission.cryptominer.title: Night Shift
mission.cryptominer.tagline: A GPU is busy with no job scheduled. Investigate, contain and remove persistence.
mission.cryptominer.briefing:
Monitoring fired **GpuBusyWithoutJob** on **node-2**: a GPU is pegged, but Slurm says nothing is allocated there. This is a defensive incident-response drill on a simulated cluster.

Contain it properly:
1. **Stop the unauthorized workload.**
2. **Close the way in.** Something on node-2 is exposed to the network.
3. **Lock the compromised account.**
4. **Remove persistence**, so it doesn't come back by itself.

The objective only completes once the GPU stays clean for **2 minutes**. Useful: `ssh node-2`, `nvidia-smi`, `ps aux`, `ss -tnp`, `systemctl`, `journalctl -u <svc>`, `crontab -l -u <user>`, `sudo`.
mission.cryptominer.debrief:
**What happened**: an intern started Jupyter with `--ip=0.0.0.0` and **no token or password**. Anyone who could reach port 8888 could run code as `intern`. Someone at 203.0.113.77 did: they uploaded a miner, added a **cron entry** to respawn it, and pointed it at a GPU outside Slurm's control.

**Why each step mattered**
- *Killing the process* alone fails: cron and the open notebook both bring it back.
- *Stopping the service* closes the entry point. *Locking the account* stops reuse of the identity.
- *Removing the cron entry* removes persistence.

**Prevention for a shared GPU cluster**
- Never expose notebooks directly. Tunnel over SSH or use an authenticated gateway, and firewall compute nodes.
- Enforce that GPU access goes **through the scheduler**: cgroups/device isolation so processes outside a job allocation can't open `/dev/nvidia*`.
- Alert on *GPU busy without a job*. DCGM per-process accounting plus scheduler state makes it trivial.
- Least privilege, and audit logs you actually read.

In a real incident you'd also **preserve evidence**, rotate credentials and notify your security team. Containment is step one, not the end.
mission.cryptominer.hint.0: `ssh node-2`, then `nvidia-smi` shows a process on GPU 3 that isn't `python train.py`. `ps aux` shows who owns it.
mission.cryptominer.hint.1: If you kill it, it comes back. Check `sudo crontab -l -u intern`, and `ss -tlnp` for a service listening on 0.0.0.0. Then `journalctl -u jupyter-intern`.
mission.cryptominer.hint.2: `sudo crontab -r -u intern`, `sudo systemctl disable --now jupyter-intern`, `sudo usermod -L intern`, `sudo kill -9 <pid>`.
mission.fit-70b.title: Seventy Billion Reasons
mission.fit-70b.tagline: A 70B model on 32 GPUs: it doesn't fit. Choose a parallelism strategy that does, and runs fast.
mission.fit-70b.briefing:
You have **4 nodes × 8 H100 (80 GB)** and a **70B-parameter** model to train. With plain data parallelism every GPU would need ~1.2 TB. It OOMs instantly.

Design a parallel layout that **fits in memory** and reaches **≥ 35% MFU** on all 32 GPUs. Knobs in `train.py`: `--tp` (tensor parallel), `--pp` (pipeline parallel), `--zero 0-3`, `--micro-batch`, `--grad-accum`, `--ckpt`.

Remember: *dp = 32 / (tp × pp)*, NVLink only exists **inside** a node, and 80 layers must split evenly across pipeline stages.
mission.fit-70b.debrief:
**Memory math first, then the network topology.**

- Mixed-precision Adam costs ~16 B/param: 70B × 16 = 1.1 TB of state *before* activations. Something must shard it.
- **ZeRO / FSDP** shards optimizer state, gradients and (stage 3) parameters across data-parallel ranks. Stage 3 fits anything, but the parameters must be **all-gathered every forward and backward**. Over a 400 Gb/s NIC that dominated your step.
- **Tensor parallelism** (Megatron-style) splits each matmul across GPUs. It needs ~4 activation all-reduces *per layer*, so it belongs on **NVLink inside a node**. tp=16 would push that traffic over InfiniBand.
- **Pipeline parallelism** splits the layer stack. Traffic is light, but it costs a *bubble* of (pp−1)/(microbatches+pp−1). More gradient accumulation shrinks it.

The common recipe, "TP inside the node, PP across a few nodes, DP (+ZeRO-1) across the rest", falls straight out of the bandwidth hierarchy. That's the core idea of 3D parallelism.
mission.fit-70b.objective.0: A 70B job is training on 32 GPUs without OOM
mission.fit-70b.hint.0: Read the OOM line in `slurm-101.out`: it breaks memory into weights, grads, optimizer and activations. Optimizer state is the biggest chunk.
mission.fit-70b.hint.1: ZeRO-3 across 32 GPUs fits, but it all-gathers 140 GB of parameters over InfiniBand twice per micro-batch. Try it and watch MFU. Tensor parallelism *inside* the node (tp=8, NVLink) is the classic move.
mission.fit-70b.hint.2: `--tp 8 --pp 2 --zero 1` (dp=2) or `--tp 8 --pp 1 --zero 1` (dp=4) both work. Don't set tp above 8, or tensor-parallel traffic crosses InfiniBand.
mission.pod-design.title: Build the Pod
mission.pod-design.tagline: Spec a GPU pod that trains a 13B model in two weeks, within budget and the facility's power envelope.
mission.pod-design.briefing:
Your lab won funding to pretrain a **13B model on 300B tokens**. Constraints from finance and facilities:

- **Capex ≤ $2.0M** (GPUs, hosts, network)
- **Facility power ≤ 60 kW**, including cooling (PUE 1.3)
- **Training time ≤ 14 days**

Pick the GPU, node count and network fabric. The estimate searches parallelism layouts (TP/PP/ZeRO/micro-batch) for each design and reports the best one that fits in memory. Lower energy is better. It's part of your score.
mission.pod-design.debrief:
**Architecture is a constrained optimization**, and the binding constraint moves:

- **L40S**: cheap, but PCIe-only (no NVLink) and less memory per GPU, so tensor parallelism hurts and 13B training lands well past two weeks.
- **A100**: affordable per node, but you'd need ~10+ nodes for the deadline, which breaks the budget.
- **H100 × 5–6 nodes**: makes the deadline. **Ethernet 100G** is cheaper, but gradient sync becomes exposed time and you miss the date. **RoCE 400G** is a legitimate cost-saver over InfiniBand when tuned well.

**Energy matters too**: newer GPUs often win on *joules per token* even when they draw more watts, because they finish so much sooner. Report MWh and CO₂e with every design review.
mission.pod-design.hint.0: Total FLOPs ≈ 6 × 13e9 × 300e9 ≈ 2.3e22. Divide by (GPUs × peak × ~55% MFU) for a quick sanity check.
mission.pod-design.hint.1: A100s are cheap per GPU but deliver ~1/3 of H100 throughput. Count how many nodes you'd need, and what that costs.
mission.pod-design.hint.2: Try 5–6 H100 nodes. Then compare InfiniBand, RoCE and 100 GbE Ethernet: gradient sync over TCP-class networks shows up in the time.
cp.gpu.0.prompt: How does a GPU mainly hide memory latency?
cp.gpu.0.explain: GPUs trade single-thread speed for parallelism: while one warp waits on memory, the scheduler issues another.
cp.gpu.0.opt.1: Keeping thousands of threads in flight and switching between them
cp.gpu.0.opt.2: A bigger L3 cache than CPUs
cp.gpu.1.prompt: Roughly how much slower is PCIe Gen5 (~64 GB/s) than an H100's HBM (~3,350 GB/s)?
cp.gpu.1.explain: 3350 ÷ 64 ≈ 52. That's why data should stay on the device instead of shuttling over PCIe.
cp.streaming-multiprocessor.0.prompt: nvidia-smi reports 100% GPU-Util. What does that actually guarantee?
cp.streaming-multiprocessor.0.explain: GPU-Util only means some kernel was active. Use DCGM's SM_ACTIVE / tensor-pipe metrics to measure real saturation.
cp.streaming-multiprocessor.0.opt.1: A kernel was running during the sample window
cp.streaming-multiprocessor.1.prompt: An H100 is thermally throttled to 55% of its max SM clock. Roughly what percent of its peak FLOP/s can it deliver?
cp.streaming-multiprocessor.1.explain: Peak FLOP/s = SMs × FLOPs/clock × clock, so throughput scales with clock: ~55%.
cp.hbm.0.prompt: Mixed-precision Adam needs ~16 bytes per parameter. How many GB of state does a 7-billion-parameter model need, before activations?
cp.hbm.0.explain: 7e9 × 16 B = 112 GB, more than an 80 GB GPU holds, which is why we shard (ZeRO) or split (TP/PP).
cp.hbm.1.prompt: A kernel does one addition for every 8 bytes it reads from memory. What limits its speed on an H100?
cp.hbm.1.explain: Arithmetic intensity ≈ 0.125 FLOP/byte, far below the ridge point (~295). It's memory-bound.
cp.pcie.0.prompt: `nvidia-smi topo -m` shows `SYS` between every pair of GPUs (no NVLink). Which parallelism suffers most?
cp.pcie.0.explain: Tensor parallelism needs several all-reduces per layer. Over PCIe through the CPU that becomes the bottleneck.
cp.pcie.1.prompt: Xid 79 says the GPU has "fallen off the bus". Which bus?
cp.pcie.1.explain: The driver can no longer reach the GPU over PCIe. That's a reboot at minimum, often a hardware ticket.
cp.nvlink.0.prompt: Which parallelism should live inside the NVLink domain?
cp.nvlink.0.explain: Put the chattiest traffic on the fastest link: TP all-reduces activations every layer.
cp.nvlink.1.prompt: Given this output, which Xid would you expect in `dmesg`?
cp.nvlink.1.explain: Xid 74 is an NVLink error. Traffic quietly falls back to PCIe and collectives slow down.
cp.nvswitch.0.prompt: What does NVSwitch add on top of point-to-point NVLink?
cp.nvswitch.0.explain: Without a switch, each GPU links to only a few neighbors. NVSwitch builds a non-blocking crossbar.
cp.nvswitch.0.opt.3: Links to other servers over InfiniBand
cp.nvswitch.1.prompt: `nvidia-smi topo -m` shows `NV18` between every pair of GPUs. What does 18 mean?
cp.nvswitch.1.explain: NV# is the number of bonded NVLinks: 18 on an H100 SXM, about 900 GB/s bidirectional.
cp.infiniband.0.prompt: You see this in a multi-node job log. What's happening?
cp.infiniband.0.explain: NET/Socket means TCP. Remove NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1 to get NET/IB (RDMA).
cp.infiniband.0.opt.0: All good: RDMA is in use
cp.infiniband.0.opt.1: NCCL fell back to TCP sockets, so expect a big slowdown
cp.infiniband.0.opt.3: The job is out of memory
cp.infiniband.1.prompt: In a rail-optimized H100 server, roughly how much scale-out bandwidth does each GPU get?
cp.infiniband.1.explain: 400 Gb/s ÷ 8 bits = 50 GB/s per GPU, about a ninth of NVLink.
cp.cluster-topology.0.prompt: Why does network oversubscription (e.g. 2:1) hurt training more than web traffic?
cp.cluster-topology.0.explain: Collectives are bursty and synchronized. Everyone needs full bandwidth at the same moment.
cp.cluster-topology.0.opt.1: During all-reduce every GPU transmits at the same time
cp.cluster-topology.1.prompt: Order the bandwidth hierarchy, fastest first:
cp.cluster-topology.1.explain: ~3.35 TB/s HBM, ~450 GB/s NVLink, ~50 GB/s per-GPU InfiniBand, then storage. Map parallelism onto it.
cp.cuda-stack.0.prompt: A container ships the CUDA 12.4 runtime, but the host driver only supports up to CUDA 12.2. What happens?
cp.cuda-stack.0.explain: A newer driver runs older runtimes, not the reverse. nvidia-smi shows the max CUDA version the driver supports.
cp.cuda-stack.0.opt.0: Works fine: newer runtimes always run on older drivers
cp.cuda-stack.0.opt.1: It will likely fail: the driver must support the runtime's CUDA version (unless forward-compat packages are used)
cp.cuda-stack.0.opt.2: The container installs its own kernel driver
cp.cuda-stack.1.prompt: Where do Xid messages come from?
cp.cuda-stack.1.explain: The kernel module (open-gpu-kernel-modules) logs them to the kernel log: dmesg / journalctl -k.
cp.slurm.0.prompt: Nodes have 8 GPUs and the script asks for `--gpus-per-node=16`. What's the most likely cause of this error?
cp.slurm.0.explain: Slurm rejects requests no node can ever satisfy. Ask for 2 nodes × 8 GPUs instead.
cp.slurm.0.opt.1: It requests more GPUs per node than any node has
cp.slurm.1.prompt: You suspect node-3's hardware. What's the polite way to take it out of service?
cp.slurm.1.explain: Drain lets running jobs finish, keeps new ones away, and records why in `sinfo -R`.
cp.slurm.1.opt.1: scontrol update NodeName=node-3 State=DRAIN Reason="gpu5 fan"
cp.nccl.0.prompt: Which environment variable makes NCCL print the transport it chose?
cp.nccl.0.explain: NCCL_DEBUG=INFO logs NET/IB vs NET/Socket, channels and topology. Read it when a job is slow.
cp.nccl.1.prompt: A job hangs, then dies with a ProcessGroupNCCL watchdog timeout. What's the most likely cause?
cp.nccl.1.explain: Collectives are barriers. One missing rank stalls everyone until the watchdog fires.
cp.nccl.1.opt.1: One rank stopped responding (dead link, lost GPU, or a straggler)
cp.checkpointing.0.prompt: Young/Daly: interval ≈ √(2 × checkpoint cost × MTBF). A checkpoint takes 2 minutes and MTBF is 4 hours. Interval in minutes?
cp.checkpointing.1.prompt: A job is requeued after a node failure. Where does it resume?
cp.checkpointing.1.explain: Work since the last checkpoint is lost. That's why the interval matters.
cp.kubernetes-gpu.0.prompt: Distributed training on Kubernetes needs gang scheduling. Why?
cp.kubernetes-gpu.0.explain: Kubernetes schedules pods one by one. Add-ons like Kueue or Volcano provide all-or-nothing placement.
cp.kubernetes-gpu.0.opt.1: All workers must start together or not at all, because partial starts deadlock
cp.kubernetes-gpu.1.prompt: Which component advertises `nvidia.com/gpu` to the Kubernetes scheduler?
cp.kubernetes-gpu.1.explain: The device plugin (usually installed by the GPU Operator) exposes GPUs as a schedulable resource.
cp.fair-share.0.prompt: Team A used 3× its share last week. Under fair-share scheduling, its new jobs…
cp.fair-share.0.explain: Priority drops with recent usage and recovers as it decays (e.g. a 7-day half-life).
cp.fair-share.0.opt.1: get lower priority until the usage decays
cp.fair-share.1.prompt: Preemption works well only if jobs…
cp.fair-share.1.explain: A preempted job restarts from its last checkpoint. Rare checkpoints waste a lot of work.
cp.nvidia-smi.0.prompt: This GPU draws 437 W while its neighbors draw ~650 W at the same job. Which command shows *why*?
cp.nvidia-smi.0.explain: The PERFORMANCE section lists Clocks Event Reasons: power cap, HW slowdown, thermal slowdown.
cp.nvidia-smi.1.prompt: Which nvidia-smi flag sets a GPU power limit?
cp.nvidia-smi.1.explain: `sudo nvidia-smi -pl 550` (add `-i <gpu>` for one GPU). -r resets, -L lists, -q queries.
cp.power-and-thermals.0.explain: HW Thermal Slowdown is the emergency brake for heat. A power cap would show SW Power Cap.
cp.power-and-thermals.0.opt.1: Overheating (a failed fan or blocked airflow)
cp.power-and-thermals.1.prompt: In synchronous training, one GPU drops to 55% clock. Whole-job throughput becomes roughly…
cp.power-and-thermals.1.explain: Every collective waits for the slowest GPU, so the whole job runs at the straggler's pace.
cp.xid-errors.0.prompt: You find this in dmesg on node-2. What's the right first response?
cp.xid-errors.0.explain: Contain first (drain), recover (requeue from checkpoint), then diagnose the hardware offline.
cp.xid-errors.0.opt.0: Restart the job on the same node
cp.xid-errors.0.opt.1: Drain the node with the Xid in the reason and requeue the job elsewhere
cp.xid-errors.1.explain: Those are typically user-code faults. Check the job before blaming the GPU.
cp.xid-errors.1.opt.1: The application's code (bad memory access, illegal instruction)
