cp.ecc-errors.0.explain: Row remapping takes effect at the next reset: drain, wait for jobs, `nvidia-smi -r -i <gpu>`, then run diagnostics.
cp.ecc-errors.0.opt.1: A GPU reset once it's idle
cp.ecc-errors.1.explain: A slowly rising count is normal. A rapidly rising one is an early warning.
cp.ecc-errors.1.opt.1: Corrected on the fly and counted
cp.dcgm.0.prompt: Which alert catches both leaked processes and cryptominers?
cp.dcgm.0.explain: Compare DCGM utilization with scheduler state. Busy with no job means something is running that shouldn't be.
cp.dcgm.0.opt.1: GPU busy while the scheduler shows no job on that node
cp.dcgm.1.prompt: A node is back from hardware repair. Before it rejoins the pool, run…
cp.dcgm.1.explain: Level 3 diagnostics include stress tests. Level 1 is the quick deployment check.
cp.stragglers.0.explain: Low clock with high utilization: it's the one everyone else is waiting for.
cp.stragglers.1.prompt: Why do the healthy GPUs show *lower* utilization during a straggler event?
cp.stragglers.1.explain: Inverted utilization (one pegged, the rest lower) is the classic straggler signature.
cp.stragglers.1.opt.1: They finish early and wait at the barrier for the slow GPU
cp.warp.0.prompt: How many threads are in an NVIDIA warp?
cp.warp.1.prompt: Half the threads in a warp take the `if` branch and half take the `else`. What happens?
cp.warp.1.explain: Branch divergence serializes the paths. Keep control flow uniform within a warp.
cp.warp.1.opt.0: Both halves run in parallel at full speed
cp.warp.1.opt.1: The warp runs both paths with lanes masked off, taking roughly 2× the time
cp.memory-coalescing.0.prompt: 32 threads in a warp read 32 consecutive 4-byte floats. How many 128-byte memory transactions does that need?
cp.memory-coalescing.0.explain: 32 × 4 = 128 bytes, fully coalesced into one transaction. A large stride could need 32.
cp.memory-coalescing.1.prompt: Which data layout helps coalescing when kernels touch one field at a time?
cp.memory-coalescing.1.explain: With SoA, thread i reads element i of the same field, so the reads are adjacent.
cp.occupancy.0.prompt: What limits how many warps can be resident on an SM?
cp.occupancy.0.explain: The register file and shared memory are split among resident warps.
cp.occupancy.0.opt.0: Registers per thread, shared memory per block, and threads/blocks per SM
cp.occupancy.1.explain: GEMMs and FlashAttention often run at low occupancy. Measure, don't assume.
cp.occupancy.1.opt.1: No: many top kernels trade occupancy for data reuse in registers and shared memory
cp.tensor-core.0.prompt: An H100 does ~989 dense BF16 TFLOP/s on tensor cores versus ~67 TFLOP/s plain FP32. Roughly how many times faster?
cp.tensor-core.0.explain: 989 ÷ 67 ≈ 14.8, which is why training in plain FP32 leaves most of the GPU idle.
cp.tensor-core.1.prompt: Which of these hurts tensor core efficiency?
cp.tensor-core.1.explain: Small matrices can't fill the tensor core tiles and pipelines.
cp.tensor-core.1.opt.1: Tiny micro-batches and very narrow tensor-parallel shards
cp.mixed-precision.0.prompt: Why does BF16 rarely need loss scaling, while FP16 does?
cp.mixed-precision.0.explain: BF16's 8-bit exponent matches FP32's range, so small gradients don't underflow.
cp.mixed-precision.1.prompt: In mixed-precision training, what is kept in FP32?
cp.mixed-precision.1.explain: 2 B weights + 2 B grads + 12 B FP32 optimizer state gives the 16 bytes/param rule.
cp.mixed-precision.1.opt.1: Master weights (plus Adam moments) for the optimizer update
cp.data-parallelism.0.prompt: With ring all-reduce, what happens to per-GPU gradient traffic as you add GPUs?
cp.data-parallelism.0.explain: 2(n−1)/n × S approaches 2S. That's why data parallelism scales so well.
cp.data-parallelism.0.opt.1: It stays roughly constant (~2× the gradient size)
cp.data-parallelism.1.explain: Several micro-batches, one sync. Fewer bytes on the wire per token.
cp.data-parallelism.1.opt.1: grow the global batch without more memory, and sync less often per token
cp.cuda-streams.0.prompt: Which PyTorch habit silently kills compute/communication overlap?
cp.cuda-streams.0.explain: .item() forces a device sync, collapsing async streams back into serial execution.
cp.cuda-streams.1.prompt: How does grCUDA run independent kernels concurrently without hand-written streams?
cp.cuda-streams.1.explain: It builds a dependency graph from kernel arguments and schedules independent work on separate streams.
cp.cuda-streams.1.opt.1: It infers dependencies from the data each kernel touches
cp.cuda-streams.1.opt.2: It runs them on the CPU
cp.activation-checkpointing.0.prompt: Full checkpointing costs an extra forward pass: 8N instead of 6N FLOPs per token. How much extra compute, in %?
cp.activation-checkpointing.0.explain: 8 ÷ 6 = 1.33, so ~33% more compute in exchange for much less activation memory.
cp.activation-checkpointing.1.prompt: Memory is comfortable, MFU is low, and activation checkpointing is on. What should you try?
cp.activation-checkpointing.1.explain: When activations fit, recomputation is pure overhead.
cp.zero-fsdp.0.prompt: ZeRO-1 with dp = 8 shards only the 12 B/param optimizer state. Per-GPU state in bytes per parameter (2 weights + 2 grads + 12/8)?
cp.zero-fsdp.1.prompt: Why can ZeRO-3 / FSDP be slow across nodes?
cp.zero-fsdp.1.explain: For 70B that's ~140 GB moved twice per micro-batch. That's fine on NVLink, painful over a 400G NIC.
cp.zero-fsdp.1.opt.1: It all-gathers parameters before every forward and backward of every micro-batch
cp.tensor-parallelism.0.prompt: Why keep tensor parallelism ≤ 8 on HGX servers?
cp.tensor-parallelism.0.explain: An HGX NVLink domain is 8 GPUs. Past it, latency-critical traffic hits the slower fabric.
cp.tensor-parallelism.0.opt.1: TP's per-layer all-reduces need NVLink; beyond 8 GPUs they cross InfiniBand
cp.tensor-parallelism.1.prompt: Megatron-style TP needs how many activation all-reduces per transformer layer per micro-batch (forward + backward)?
cp.tensor-parallelism.1.explain: One for attention and one for the MLP in forward, and the same again in backward.
cp.pipeline-parallelism.0.prompt: p = 4 pipeline stages, m = 12 micro-batches per step. Bubble fraction (p−1)/(m+p−1), in %?
cp.pipeline-parallelism.0.explain: 3 ÷ 15 = 20% of the step is idle fill and drain.
cp.pipeline-parallelism.1.prompt: How do you shrink the pipeline bubble?
cp.pipeline-parallelism.1.explain: More micro-batches (gradient accumulation) amortize fill and drain. Interleaved schedules help too.
cp.roofline.0.prompt: H100 BF16: 989 TFLOP/s peak and 3.35 TB/s HBM. Where's the ridge point, in FLOPs per byte?
cp.roofline.0.explain: 989e12 ÷ 3.35e12 ≈ 295. Below it you're memory-bound, above it compute-bound.
cp.roofline.1.prompt: A kernel with arithmetic intensity 10 runs on an H100. It can reach about…
cp.roofline.1.explain: min(989, 10 × 3.35) = 33.5 TFLOP/s. Fusing ops raises intensity.
cp.mfu.0.prompt: A 7B model trains at 500k tokens/s on 32 H100s (989 TFLOP/s each). MFU = 6·N·tokens/s ÷ (GPUs × peak). In %?
cp.mfu.1.prompt: Do recomputed FLOPs from activation checkpointing count toward MFU?
cp.mfu.1.explain: MFU only rewards useful model FLOPs, so it can't be gamed with recomputation.
cp.mfu.1.opt.1: No: counting them gives HFU (hardware FLOPs utilization)
cp.all-reduce.0.prompt: Ring all-reduce of 1 GB across 8 GPUs at 100 GB/s per link, ignoring latency: 2(n−1)/n · S/B. Time in ms?
cp.all-reduce.1.prompt: Tree all-reduce algorithms beat rings mainly for…
cp.all-reduce.1.explain: Trees need ~log₂(n) latency steps instead of ~2(n−1).
cp.all-reduce.1.opt.0: Huge messages on a few GPUs
cp.all-reduce.1.opt.1: Small messages at large scale, where latency dominates
cp.scaling-efficiency.0.prompt: Amdahl's law: 5% of the work is serial. What's the maximum speedup, even with infinite GPUs?
cp.scaling-efficiency.1.prompt: 1 GPU does 10k tokens/s; 64 GPUs do 512k tokens/s. Scaling efficiency, in %?
cp.input-pipeline.0.prompt: Your job log says this. What's the best first fix?
cp.input-pipeline.0.explain: The GPUs are waiting on the CPU-side input pipeline, so feed them faster.
cp.input-pipeline.0.opt.0: More dataloader workers, or pre-tokenized data
cp.input-pipeline.1.prompt: Each worker tokenizes 8k tokens/s. A rank needs 64k tokens per 1-second step. Minimum number of workers?
cp.power-capping.0.prompt: Why does a power cap cost less performance than the power it saves?
cp.power-capping.0.explain: The last few hundred MHz are the most expensive, so dropping them saves a lot of watts.
cp.power-capping.0.opt.0: Dynamic power ∝ f·V², and voltage has to rise with frequency
cp.power-capping.1.prompt: You cap only 1 of the 16 GPUs in a training job. What happens?
cp.power-capping.1.explain: Synchronous training runs at the slowest GPU's pace. Cap them all evenly.
cp.power-capping.1.opt.0: Saves 1/16 of the power at no cost
cp.power-capping.1.opt.1: Creates a straggler that slows all 16
cp.energy-and-carbon.0.prompt: IT load of 100 kW, PUE 1.3, running for 24 hours. Facility energy in MWh?
cp.energy-and-carbon.1.prompt: 3,000 kWh on a grid at 0.4 kg CO₂e per kWh. How many kg of CO₂e?
cp.energy-and-carbon.1.explain: 3,000 × 0.4 = 1,200 kg. The same job in a cleaner region could be several times lower.
cp.containers-and-gpus.0.prompt: When a container uses a GPU, where does the kernel driver come from?
cp.containers-and-gpus.0.explain: Images carry the CUDA runtime; the driver (a kernel module) always comes from the host.
cp.containers-and-gpus.0.opt.1: The host, injected by the NVIDIA Container Toolkit
cp.containers-and-gpus.1.explain: Privileged containers can escape to the host. GPU access doesn't need it.
cp.containers-and-gpus.1.opt.1: No: grant device access narrowly through the runtime
cp.multi-tenancy.0.prompt: Which way of sharing a GPU gives hardware-isolated memory and SMs?
cp.multi-tenancy.0.explain: MIG partitions SMs, L2 and memory controllers. MPS and time-slicing share them.
cp.multi-tenancy.1.prompt: What's the best way to ensure GPUs are only used through the scheduler?
cp.multi-tenancy.1.explain: Enforcement beats policy: processes outside an allocation simply can't open the device.
cp.multi-tenancy.1.opt.1: cgroup device controls restricting /dev/nvidia* to job allocations
cp.mig.0.prompt: What's the maximum number of MIG instances on an H100?
cp.mig.0.explain: Seven compute slices, so up to seven 1g instances.
cp.mig.1.prompt: Can a 3g.40gb and a 4g.40gb instance fit together on one 80 GB H100 (7 compute slices, 8 memory slices)?
cp.mig.1.explain: 3 + 4 = 7 compute slices and 4 + 4 = 8 memory slices. A perfect fit.
cp.mig.1.opt.0: Yes: together they use exactly 7 compute and 8 memory slices
cp.exposed-notebooks.0.prompt: Why is this alarming on a compute node?
cp.exposed-notebooks.0.explain: 0.0.0.0 means reachable from the network. Without a token, anyone can run code as that user.
cp.exposed-notebooks.0.opt.1: A notebook server (remote code execution) is listening on all interfaces
cp.exposed-notebooks.1.prompt: What's a safer way to use Jupyter on a cluster?
cp.exposed-notebooks.1.explain: Keep it local and authenticated: SSH tunnels or JupyterHub with SSO.
cp.exposed-notebooks.1.opt.1: Bind to 127.0.0.1 and use an SSH tunnel or an authenticated gateway
cp.cryptojacking.0.prompt: You kill a miner process and it reappears a minute later. What do you check first?
cp.cryptojacking.0.explain: Something is restarting it. Remove the persistence and close the door it came in through.
cp.cryptojacking.0.opt.1: Persistence (cron entries, systemd units) and the original entry point
cp.cryptojacking.1.prompt: Outbound connections to which ports often indicate mining-pool (stratum) traffic?
cp.cryptojacking.1.explain: Stratum pools commonly use ports like 3333, 4444 and 5555. Watch for them in `ss -tnp` and firewall logs.
cp.supply-chain-and-secrets.0.prompt: Which format is safer for downloaded model weights?
cp.supply-chain-and-secrets.0.explain: Loading a pickle can execute arbitrary code. safetensors is plain tensor data.
cp.supply-chain-and-secrets.1.prompt: Where should a job's cloud credentials come from?
cp.supply-chain-and-secrets.1.explain: Short-lived, least-privilege secrets injected at runtime never end up in images or git history.
cp.supply-chain-and-secrets.1.opt.2: A secret manager, injected at runtime and scoped to the job
